title: Slow is fast: raising barriers to accelerate thermal relaxation
abstract: For a reversible system relaxing to equilibrium, the obvious fastest strategy is to lower all kinetic barriers (open all gates). We find that such intuition holds at three levels: the all-open-gate strategy achieves the highest local conductance, it maximizes the instantaneous speed of approach in every $f$-divergence, and it simultaneously maximizes all relaxation eigenvalues. Nevertheless, we show that a counter-intuitive finite-time optimum lies beyond this intuition and operates at a fourth level, invisible to all three: eigenvector rotation. Noncommutativity enables timed schedules to reproject residual amplitudes across relaxation modes, thereby achieving faster relaxation. Optimal schedules are bang--bang. In our illustrative example, the best-found schedule also employs counter-gating, transiently raising selected barriers, and reduces the terminal residual by a factor of $130$ relative to all-open, and by $7$ relative to the best static landscape. A no-go theorem shows that noncommutativity is necessary: commuting generators collapse every schedule to a static time-averaged landscape, worse than the intuitive static control. In the reverse problem, the dual schedule preserves nonequilibrium free energy far more effectively than intuitively keeping all barriers at maximum heights. Whether accelerating or delaying relaxation, barrier control performs no work on the reduced Markov system; it only re-times a fixed total dissipation budget.
summary: The paper investigates non-equilibrium control by scheduling kinetic barriers during system relaxation. It shows that the intuitive fastest strategy (all gates open) is suboptimal because it ignores the time ordering of underlying physical processes. Optimal acceleration requires a counter-intuitive 'counter-gating' schedule, proving that the noncommutativity of the relaxation generators is key to achieving speedups.
main_problem: To determine how dynamically scheduling kinetic barriers during relaxation can accelerate or slow down the approach to equilibrium without performing external work.
main_result: Optimal schedules require non-commuting time ordering of barrier control, enabling 'counter-gating' (transiently raising some barriers) to achieve faster relaxation than simply keeping all gates open.
method: The analysis uses optimal control theory (Pontryagin's principle) applied to the evolution governed by a time-dependent Lindblad/Master equation, analyzing the terminal distance using f-divergences like $\chi^2$.
model_or_system: A reversible system relaxing to equilibrium described by a connected graph of states. The dynamics are controlled by modulating kinetic barriers $B_e(t)$ via time-dependent conductances $g_e(t) = \exp[- eta B_e(t)]$.
key_observables: Terminal distance from equilibrium ($\chi^2(T)$), relaxation eigenvalues ($\gamma_a$), and the entropy production rate $\sigma(t)$.
important_parameters: The control schedule $\{y_e(t)\}$, which dictates barrier heights, and the finite time $T$ at which the measurement is taken.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the modulation of barriers is slow compared to fast intrawell equilibration; it also relies on the system being reversible and having fixed initial/final states (no work done).
figures_summary: Figures compare relaxation performance ($\chi^2(T)$) for various protocols, showing that time-ordered gating significantly outperforms static 'all-open' or 'all-high' controls.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the benchmark (all-open gates), introduces the finite-time optimization problem using control theory, derives necessary conditions via Pontryagin's principle, and proves that noncommutativity is essential for achieving acceleration through counter-gating.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical framework for understanding how temporal ordering of microscopic processes (like opening/closing gates) can fundamentally alter macroscopic relaxation dynamics, which has implications for quantum thermalization and energy transport in complex systems.
